publishedSummary: The breast is a modified sweat gland lying in the superficial fascia of the chest wall. Almost everything clinically important about it — how it is supported, how it changes, where its cancers spread — follows from that developmental origin and that position.
holdThese: The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland, developing from an epidermal downgrowth into underlying connective tissue.
It lies in the superficial fascia, not within the pectoral muscles, so it moves independently of them.
Being a skin gland, it is a branching duct system opening onto the surface at the nipple.
Its secretion is apocrine-like, unlike the merocrine secretion of ordinary sweat glands.
Its skin-gland origin explains why breast tissue may appear anywhere along the embryonic milk line.

sections.narrative:
The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland. That single statement of origin organises most of what follows. Like other skin appendages, it begins as a downgrowth of surface epidermis into the connective tissue beneath, and it retains the basic architecture of such a gland throughout life: a branching system of ducts leading from secretory units to an opening on the skin surface. What distinguishes it is scale and specialisation — the secretory units are elaborated into lobules, the secretion is milk rather than sweat, and the mode of secretion is apocrine-like rather than the simple merocrine secretion of an ordinary sweat gland.

Because it is a skin gland, it stays with the skin. The breast lies within the superficial fascia of the anterior chest wall, superficial to the deep fascia covering pectoralis major, and separated from it by a plane of loose tissue. It is not part of the muscle, and it normally moves over the muscle rather than with it. That plane is why a normal breast can be lifted freely from the chest wall, and why loss of that mobility on examination is significant: it indicates that a process has crossed out of the gland into the tissue behind.

The skin-gland origin also explains findings that would otherwise seem arbitrary. Mammary tissue develops along a paired embryonic milk line running from axilla to groin, and because the gland arises from surface ectoderm along that line, accessory nipples or accessory breast tissue may appear anywhere on it — most often in the axilla. Similarly, since ducts open onto the skin, disease of those ducts can present at the surface, as nipple discharge or as changes at the nipple itself.

The gland sits in fat and is crossed by fibrous septa running from the deep fascia to the skin. These give the breast its shape and its support, and because they are attached at both ends, a process that shortens them tethers the overlying skin — the mechanism behind skin dimpling.
